title: Super fund ranks tipped to halve within decade
full_text:
Australia’s superannuation sector could shrink to around 33 APRA-regulated funds by 2035 as consolidation accelerates and competitive pressure increasingly favours larger funds and platforms, according to Mercer Super.
Mercer’s Shaping Super 2026 report found the number of funds had already fallen to 75 as at 30 June 2025, below the 78 it had forecast a year earlier, with the firm expecting the decline to continue rapidly over the coming decade.
Beyond 2035, consolidation is projected to slow, leaving a median long-term estimate of about 18 funds by 2050.
The report estimated half of the mergers expected over the next 25 years would occur within the next five years, while funds holding more than $10 billion in assets today were roughly twice as likely to survive as those below that threshold.
While consolidation is expected to remove smaller players, Mercer projected the Australian super system itself would continue expanding significantly, with assets rising from $4.3 trillion at June 2025 to $5.7 trillion in 2030 and $15.1 trillion by 2050.
At that point, super assets would represent about 169 per cent of gross domestic product, with investment returns expected to account for 58 per cent of total system growth over the period and contributions supplying the remaining 42 per cent.
The increasing scale of surviving funds is also expected to reshape the market, with Mercer forecasting the average fund will quadruple to $161 billion under management by 2035.
However, the firm cautioned that scale alone would not guarantee success as an ageing population pushed more funds towards negative cash flow positions.
“While scale offers advantages, nuances in fund position mean that scale alone is not necessarily the definitive measure of success,” the report said.
“Smaller remaining funds (which are generally not so ‘small’ anymore) face headwinds, but there are benefits to being nimble with a smaller customer base. Nevertheless, for some funds, survival will be challenging and will require intentional, strategic action today to have the privilege of serving members tomorrow.”
Mercer’s modelling suggested fund size was not the only significant predictor of survival, with net account growth also playing a major role. Each percentage point increase in net account growth reduced the odds of a fund closing within the following decade by approximately 2 per cent, while expense ratios and investment returns did not show statistically significant associations with fund exits.
Competition for members has intensified following the introduction of super stapling, which reduced the flow of members through traditional employer default arrangements and pushed funds towards alternative distribution channels.
Against that backdrop, the median fund received 11 per cent of its organic flows from members joining directly in 2024–25, up from 9 per cent a year earlier, pointing to a growing emphasis on direct acquisition and marketing.
Inorganic growth has remained heavily concentrated, with just nine funds receiving all merger-related account flows during 2025. Mercer expects the pool of merger opportunities to diminish and the market to shift increasingly towards acquisitions, including larger entities actively pursuing smaller funds and potential transfers of particular member books.
The changing competitive landscape is also expected to strengthen the position of mega funds and platforms.
Mega funds currently hold around 39 per cent of market share, which Mercer projected would rise to 54 per cent by 2035, while platforms are expected to increase their share from 10 per cent to 14 per cent.
Retirement is emerging as another key competitive battleground, with platforms attracting a disproportionately large share of members moving into retirement products. Despite platforms accounting for only 6 per cent of accounts, the report said they attracted 42 per cent of retirement account flows, compared with 31 per cent for mega funds.
With retirement products projected to grow from 18 per cent of system assets to 25 per cent by 2035, Mercer said funds would need to improve member engagement, retirement income strategies and retention to avoid losing higher-balance members as they approach retirement.
Among its priorities for 2026, Mercer identified delivering strong member outcomes, responding to regulatory changes, improving retention and retirement income strategies, strengthening distribution, simplifying products, updating operating models and making greater use of data and AI.
